blocks.content: A Service's cluster IP resolves correctly through CoreDNS, and kube proxy routes traffic correctly to a Pod. Between those two facts sits one more object, quietly doing the actual bookkeeping neither of them owns. That object is Endpoints.
Endpoint, Given Its Own Full Depth
blocks.text: Endpoint, Given Its Own Full Depth

blocks.content: An Endpoints object is a Kubernetes resource that tracks the actual, current list of Pod IP addresses and ports that a specific Service's label selector currently matches, kept continuously up to date as Pods come and go.

For every ordinary Service with a selector, Kubernetes automatically creates and maintains a matching Endpoints object of the exact same name, without any manual action required from whoever created the Service.

This Endpoints object is the actual, concrete data structure that kube proxy reads when installing its routing rules, and that CoreDNS reads when answering a Headless Service's DNS lookup with individual Pod addresses.

Understanding Endpoints closes the final gap in the picture: a Service defines the intent, its selector, and its port, while its Endpoints object records the current, literal reality of which Pods are actually eligible to receive traffic.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784642060899-787470350.png
blocks.alt: Endpoint given its own full depth

blocks.content: Tracking Exactly Which Pod IPs Back a Service
blocks.text: Tracking Exactly Which Pod IPs Back a Service

blocks.content: The Endpoints controller, running as part of the control plane, continuously watches both Services and Pods, and whenever a Pod's labels or readiness status changes, it recalculates which Endpoints objects need to be updated.

Only Pods that are currently considered ready, meaning they have passed any configured readiness checks, are included in a Service's Endpoints object, which is precisely why an unhealthy Pod stops receiving traffic automatically.

This automatic exclusion of not ready Pods is a critical, easy to overlook safety mechanism: a Pod that is technically running but not yet able to serve traffic correctly never appears in Endpoints, and therefore never receives real requests.

This update happens continuously and automatically. There is no manual step anywhere in this process, and no engineer ever needs to directly edit an Endpoints object during normal, day to day cluster operation.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784642062557-203398681.png
blocks.alt: Tracking exactly which Pod IPs back a Service

blocks.content: A Real Endpoints Example

Returning to the payment Service from the first topic in this module, running three replicas, running kubectl get endpoints payment-service shows a list of exactly three IP address and port pairs, one for each currently ready Pod.

If one of those three Pods fails a readiness check, perhaps because a dependency it needs became temporarily unavailable, that specific Pod's IP address disappears from the Endpoints list within seconds, even though the Pod itself is still running.

Traffic destined for the payment Service is now only routed to the remaining two ready Pods, since kube proxy's routing rules are derived directly from this updated Endpoints list, not from the Service's selector definition alone.

Once the struggling Pod's dependency recovers and its readiness check begins passing again, its IP address reappears in the Endpoints list automatically, and it resumes receiving its share of traffic without any manual intervention.

$ kubectl get endpoints payment-service
NAME               ENDPOINTS                                         AGE
payment-service    10.244.1.12:8080,10.244.2.7:8080,10.244.3.9:8080  4h

blocks.content: Recap: Selectors Already Covered in Pods
blocks.text: Recap: Selectors Already Covered in Pods

blocks.content: The Pods module, back in this course, introduced label selectors as the mechanism used to query and match a set of resources by their labels, at the time in the context of a controller finding the Pods it is responsible for.

Endpoints objects are the direct, concrete result of applying that exact same selector mechanism to a Service's spec.selector field, producing a real, literal list of matching Pod addresses rather than an abstract query.

Seeing this connection makes the entire chain click into place: a Service's selector is a query, and the Endpoints object is the continuously refreshed answer to that query, kept current automatically as the underlying Pods change.

This is a genuinely satisfying moment in learning Kubernetes: a mechanism learned early, in an entirely different context, turns out to be exactly the same mechanism quietly powering something covered much later.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784642065845-975112802.png
blocks.alt: Recap of selectors already covered in Pods

blocks.content: Automatically Created, Rarely Hand Written

For the overwhelming majority of Services, an Endpoints object is never written by hand. It is created and maintained entirely automatically by Kubernetes the moment a Service with a selector is created.

The rare exception is a Service created deliberately without a selector, in which case an engineer can manually create and manage a matching Endpoints object directly, pointing it at addresses that exist entirely outside the cluster's own Pods.

This manual pattern is occasionally used to integrate a genuinely external system into the cluster's service discovery mechanism in a way that behaves like an ordinary Service, distinct from the DNS only approach ExternalName uses instead.

For nearly every practical, everyday use case covered throughout this course, however, Endpoints objects should be treated as fully automatic, read only infrastructure, inspected for debugging but never edited directly.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784642067655-764704821.png
blocks.alt: An Endpoints object created automatically by Kubernetes

blocks.content: A Common Mistake: Assuming Endpoints Always Exist
blocks.text: A Common Mistake: Assuming Endpoints Always Exist

blocks.content: A common and genuinely useful debugging mistake to learn from is assuming a Service with zero matching Pods still has some kind of meaningful Endpoints object, when in fact an Endpoints object with zero entries is a completely valid and common state.

This zero entry state occurs whenever a Service's selector does not currently match any ready Pod, whether because a typo exists in the selector's labels, because a Deployment has zero replicas, or because every matching Pod is currently failing readiness.

The fastest possible diagnosis for a Service that seems unreachable, faster than checking DNS, faster than checking kube proxy, is simply running kubectl get endpoints for that Service and confirming whether the list is empty.

An empty Endpoints list is not a Kubernetes malfunction. It is Kubernetes correctly reporting that there is genuinely nothing currently eligible to receive traffic, and the root cause lies with the selector or the Pods, not the Service object itself.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784642069466-392449165.png
blocks.alt: The mistake of assuming a Service with no matching Pods has Endpoints

blocks.content: Endpoints During a Rolling Update

During a rolling update, covered back in the Deployments module, the Endpoints object for a Service is updated continuously and incrementally as old Pods terminate and new Pods become ready, one small batch at a time.

This continuous updating is exactly what makes rolling updates appear seamless to callers: at every single moment during the rollout, the Endpoints list contains a mix of ready old and ready new Pods, never an empty or broken state.

Watching kubectl get endpoints --watch during an active rolling update is a genuinely useful way to see this mechanism directly, observing individual Pod addresses appear and disappear from the list in real time as the rollout proceeds.

This observability is one of the most concrete, hands on ways to build real confidence that a rolling update is behaving correctly, beyond simply trusting that the Deployment controller is doing the right thing invisibly.
Endpoints and Readiness Probes Working Together
blocks.text: Endpoints and Readiness Probes Working Together

blocks.content: Readiness probes, the mechanism a container uses to signal whether it is currently able to serve traffic, are the direct input the Endpoints controller relies on when deciding whether to include a Pod's address in a Service's Endpoints list.

A Pod without any readiness probe configured is considered ready the moment its containers start, which can be a problem for applications with a genuine warm up period, such as loading a large cache into memory before being able to serve requests correctly.

Configuring an accurate readiness probe, one that only reports success once the application is genuinely able to handle traffic, is directly what keeps Endpoints, and therefore all real traffic, correctly excluding a Pod during its warm up window.
This tight coupling between readiness probes and Endpoints is a recurring, foundational theme that will be covered in even greater depth later in this course, in the dedicated Health Checks module.
A Real Readiness and Endpoints Example
blocks.text: A Real Readiness and Endpoints Example

blocks.content: Consider an application Pod that takes fifteen seconds after starting to finish loading a large in memory cache, during which time it cannot correctly answer real requests, even though its process is technically running the entire time.

With a correctly configured readiness probe checking a dedicated health endpoint, that Pod is excluded from its Service's Endpoints list for those first fifteen seconds, then automatically included the moment the readiness probe begins succeeding.

Without that readiness probe, the Pod would have been included in Endpoints immediately upon starting, and a portion of real user traffic would have been routed to it during those fifteen seconds, receiving errors or extremely slow responses.

This single example demonstrates concretely why Endpoints and readiness probes should always be considered together, as one connected mechanism, rather than as two separate, unrelated Kubernetes features.

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: cache-warmed-app
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: my-app:v1
      readinessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /healthz
          port: 8080
        initialDelaySeconds: 5
        periodSeconds: 5

blocks.content: Inspecting Endpoints During an Incident

During a live production incident where a Service seems to be returning errors intermittently, comparing the current Endpoints list against the expected replica count is one of the fastest ways to confirm whether some replicas have silently dropped out.

If the Endpoints list shows fewer addresses than the Deployment's replica count, the difference directly points toward a readiness problem on the missing Pods, giving a clear, immediate direction for further investigation rather than a broad, unfocused search.

This comparison, replica count against Endpoints count, is fast enough to run in the first thirty seconds of any incident involving a suspicious Service, and it very often narrows the search dramatically before any deeper investigation is needed.

Building this specific comparison into an incident response runbook, rather than rediscovering it fresh during every incident, is a small, concrete way this topic's knowledge translates directly into faster real world incident resolution.

blocks.title: Incident Response Tip
blocks.content: Compare Endpoints count against expected replica count early in any incident involving a suspicious Service. A shortfall points directly at a readiness problem on the missing Pods.
Best Practices Around Endpoints

Treat Endpoints objects as read only diagnostic information in normal operation, using them to confirm a Service's actual current backend state rather than as something to be manually edited or managed.

Make kubectl get endpoints a habitual first step when debugging any Service that seems unreachable, since it directly reveals whether the problem lies in Pod readiness or selector matching, before investigating anything further downstream.

Pay close attention to Pod readiness checks specifically when a Service seems to be missing expected backends, since a Pod that is running but not ready is silently and correctly excluded from Endpoints.

For the rare case of manually managed Endpoints pointing at external addresses, document the reasoning clearly, since this pattern deviates from the fully automatic behavior expected of nearly every other Service in the cluster.

blocks.content: Endpoints Across Multiple Ports

For a Service exposing multiple named ports, such as the http and metrics example covered earlier in the ClusterIP topic, the corresponding Endpoints object tracks each Pod's addresses across all of those ports together in a single, unified structure.

This means a single Pod becoming not ready affects every port simultaneously. There is no mechanism for a Pod to be considered ready for one port on a multi port Service while being excluded on another port of that same Service.

Understanding this all or nothing behavior at the Pod level, rather than at the individual port level, is useful when designing readiness probes for applications that expose genuinely distinct capabilities across different ports.
In practice, this is rarely a limitation, since a single readiness probe checking overall application health is usually the correct signal for every port that same application container exposes.
Endpoints as a Building Block for Custom Tooling
blocks.text: Endpoints as a Building Block for Custom Tooling

blocks.content: Because Endpoints objects are ordinary, readable Kubernetes API resources, custom monitoring and automation tooling can watch them directly, building real time dashboards or automated alerts based on exactly how many Pods are currently backing a given Service.

This is precisely the same API that kube proxy and CoreDNS themselves consume internally, meaning any custom tooling built this way sees exactly the same live picture of Service backend health that the cluster's own core routing components rely on.

Some organizations build lightweight internal dashboards specifically around Endpoints data, giving on call engineers an immediate, at a glance view of every critical Service's actual current backend count without needing to run kubectl manually during an incident.

This extensibility is a genuinely good example of the broader Kubernetes design philosophy: nearly everything, including internal bookkeeping objects like Endpoints, is exposed through the same open, consistent API that any tool can build on top of.
The Single Most Valuable Takeaway

Endpoints is the missing piece connecting a Service's declared intent to the literal, current reality of which Pods can actually receive traffic, continuously and automatically maintained without any manual involvement in the overwhelming majority of cases.

kubectl get endpoints is one of the single most valuable, fastest diagnostic commands available for any Service related problem, and it deserves a permanent place in every engineer's early debugging checklist.

The final topic in this module, EndpointSlice, covers the modern, more scalable evolution of this exact same idea, built specifically to handle Services with very large numbers of backing Pods gracefully.

Keep the full picture assembled across this entire module in mind: a selector defines intent, Endpoints records the literal current answer, kube proxy routes according to it, and CoreDNS resolves names using the exact same underlying data.

This is a genuinely satisfying point to pause at. Every layer covered so far, from the very first topic's stable virtual IP down to this topic's literal, continuously refreshed Pod address list, now has a clear, concrete owner.

Carrying that clarity into the final topic of this module makes EndpointSlice easy to place correctly: it is not a new idea, but a scalability focused refinement of the exact mechanism just covered here.

One final, practical reminder before moving on: kubectl get endpoints is a small command with an outsized diagnostic payoff, and it belongs permanently in every engineer's first response to a Service reachability problem.

points: An Endpoints object tracks the actual, current list of ready Pod IP addresses and ports that a Service's selector matches, updated continuously and automatically.

Endpoints objects are automatically created and maintained for nearly every Service; manual management is reserved for the rare case of a selector-less Service pointing at external addresses.
kubectl get endpoints is one of the fastest, most valuable diagnostic commands for any Service reachability problem.
